title: Casual 2D Mobile game development solved
author: hydrangers
selftext:
2 months ago I decided to give AI game development a shot. I hadn't done any game development in over 15 years, so I figured it would be a fun project to kill time. I ended up recreating a game that used to be on the mobile market many years ago but had been pulled and never returned, or even cloned.

I ended up building a game where you smash ragdolls, blow them up, shoot them, freeze them, and ultimately just humiliate them for personal gain. The game is called Limb from Limb and I essentially just went into this to see how far AI has come and how capable it is with mobile game development, from design spec through to launch. Surprisingly, it was able to do pretty much everything, including submitting the game to google play and the app store.

For coding, I mostly used Claude (Fable 5 for shaders/animations, and Opus 5 for everything else), Sol 5.6 Ultra for image generation for literally all of the art, Suno for the in-game music, and elevenlabs for voices and sound effects.  
  
I think it has turned out quite nice looking for a 2d game, and fun to play for a younger audience. Let me know what you think. Again, this took 2 months to build as a 1-man show. I believe 2D game development is pretty much solved, but looking to get others opinions.

comments.author: FlipperTheRipper
comments.body:
Looks great! I making a mobile game right now but the biggest issue I’ve been having is improving the UI/UX. 

On Unity, Claude seems to struggle with using the right assets or placing them appropriately , and I always end up having to fix broken UI elements. And I suck at UI/UX dev haha

Did you develop this game on Unity? And how did you go about dealing with UI/UX?

replies.author: hydrangers
replies.body:
Thanks!  
  
Yep, I used Unity for this game. I originally started with Godot and it did fine, but moved over to Unity after I found the physics solver wasn't ideal for this type of game so I ended up switching to Unity for Box2d before I realized you can change the physics engine in Godot lol.

Surprisingly using Fable 5 for the UI was not terrible. I mostly just instructed it for each asset, for example the calendar/level selector to apply a grid overtop to properly section out and align texts before coding and positioning them. Not to say that it wasn't a struggle sometimes, and you can see it with the level failed dialog at the end of the video that they don't look super natural. A lot of the time with the rough edges of the dialogs it can get positioning wrong or just overall doesn't really make them look very good. With a couple iterations on the grid prompt and some different text styling/colors, I feel like it would be able to pass a QA check though.

As far as everything else UI/UX related, I was super detailed on how I wanted the layout to be and the design to look, for example the way the game mode and level select calendar near the start of the video how it shifts from side to side and then loads the level behind the calendar.

replies.author: HealthPuzzleheaded
replies.body:
how did you do the background?
did you instructed it to generate seperate background layers then cut those out with something like Photoshop and let claude assemple the scene?

talking mainly about the rotation of the ferriswheel

replies.author: hydrangers
replies.body:
I started with a main prompt along the lines of "generate a carnival level," and it included the Ferris wheel and carousel in the original image. Then, I proceeded to prompt it to generate the image without the Ferris wheel and carousel, and then had it generate the carousel and Ferris wheel as their own assets within the same conversation to keep consistency with the art style of the background.

From there, claude just added the assets in as layers on the level background.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Depends on which effects you like the look of the most. Your other explosions and such read to me as 'realistic', whereas the fire is a vector/toon VFX. Depending on what you find easier or more in tune with what you want, you could either take your explosions to be more looney tune style bombs with appropriate effects, and then the fire is pretty much on the mark, or you can take your fire and make it into a more traditional light/particle based effect to blend better. I think a big part is how much effort you want to put into it as you may find one style harder to universalize than the other. Particles are actually pretty easy to do procedurally, but so too can vector spritesheets depending on your workflow for them or how much knowledge you have to manually edit it (for instance I could throw a vector fire image into Krita right now and create a 16 frame spritesheet in 2 minutes. Or if I was using rigged animation just create a couple separate fire layers up and wiggle them around procedurally. However someone who has never touched a digital canvas might have no idea how to do that and be better off just asking Claude to help them design VFX (or get lucky with some GPT sprite sheets). 

Since consistency is key, it's really just about picking the route that works best for you. Since it does look like you're using rigged animations for the zombies, you could look into just replicating that for all your effects, too. Layer swaps and keyframe transformations are super easy (drop bomb sprite down, make it stutter and grow, red/white flashing filter via engine, with some flat color sparks coming off the fuse, layer swap on explosion and have 2-3 layers that show the different parts of the explosion. You get a really clean rigged animation for the bomb. And you can then reuse the same explosion with other bomb sprites (higher tier bombs or whatever). 

Unless I'm wrong and you didn't use rigged animation for your zombies. If you didn't, then learning rigged animation setups like Dragonbones or Spine or whatever might be a high ask just to get some VFX in for a game.

Game dev is just a passion that AI has helped realize (worked on games in the past, prior to AI, but the time demands were far too high to make anything of it. AI changes that. All the projects I started and never finished due to hitting bug walls or realizing I needed to refactor complex systems to avoid serious tech debt ... those are all simple to deal with now and keep that momentum going. Plus job takes a lot less time now and there are fewer clients since others are simply using AI to replace their devs. Sooo guess you could say I'm transitioning over.)

comments.author: islamoooo
comments.body:
Great work really 💯 
I was wondering is this 3D scene rendered or 2D
I noticed that you said it's AI generated assets so I assumed this is 2D but then I noticed the shadows on the grounds and walls and now I'm confused.
Are you using pre rendered scenes somehow with normal and shadow maps for this or what

replies.author: hydrangers
replies.body:
Thanks!

Pretty much all of the assets, excluding HUD items, have normal maps for lighting. The shadows are just sprites using the 2D assets for items and zombies, rendered at different angles and skewed to simulate light from the sun/moon. The moon's position is also randomized when starting a game mode, so the shadows will change based on this. I also added light sources to lightning strikes, explosions, fire, etc. So it's subtle, but zombies can actually have two separate shadows cast in different directions at different strengths based on the lighting.

I especially find it really cool to watch in slow motion when there are lots of things going on with the time slow item active!
